title: HCLTech Faces Declining Revenue From Top Clients as Google Consolidates IT Vendors
excerpt: India's third-largest IT services firm saw revenue contribution from its top five clients drop to 11.6% in Q1 FY27, continuing a downward trend as major tech clients including Google rationalize their vendor networks.
body:
• HCLTech's revenue from its top 5 clients fell from 12.6% to 11.6% over the past year, with top 10 and top 20 client buckets also shrinking — a pattern echoed across Indian IT firms.
  • Google's vendor consolidation drive is part of a wider trend among big tech companies cutting IT outsourcing costs, directly pressuring firms like HCLTech, Wipro, and Tech Mahindra.
  • HCLTech is pivoting aggressively toward AI — with $172 million in quarterly AI revenue growing 62% YoY, a $150 million Sarvam AI investment, and a ₹3,500 crore AI data centre plan — to offset top-client attrition.

Revenue From Top Clients Keeps Falling

HCLTech's Q1 FY27 investor release, filed July 13, laid bare a trend that has been building for several quarters: revenue concentration among the company's largest clients is eroding. Contribution from the top 5 clients dropped to 11.6% on a last-twelve-months basis, down from 11.9% in Q4 FY26 and 12.6% a year earlier. The top 10 bucket fell from 20.2% to 18.7%, and the top 20 from 29.9% to 28.0% over the same period.

The decline is not unique to HCLTech. Across the Indian IT sector, major firms have reported shrinking revenue from their largest accounts. Infosys saw its top 25 clients' share fall from 35.3% to 33.7%, while Wipro's top 10 contribution slid from 21.2% to 20.5%. Tech Mahindra posted the sharpest fall, with top 5 client revenue declining 16.3% year-on-year.

But for HCLTech, the sting is particularly acute because of its historically deep dependence on a handful of technology giants — with Google widely known to be among its top five accounts.

Google's Vendor Rationalization Drive

The immediate trigger is Google's ongoing consolidation of its IT services vendor network. Like many large technology companies, Google has been reducing the number of external service providers it works with, concentrating spending among fewer, larger partners while bringing some functions in-house or automating them with AI tools.

This follows a broader pattern in big tech. As Pareekh Jain, founder of Pareekh Consulting, noted in an analysis of the trend: "The three reasons for this are: ramp down of large deals, slow ramp up of large deals bagged recently, and cancellation of some projects. This is happening in a secular way, and is not limited to any particular company."

HCLTech CEO C. Vijayakumar acknowledged the pressure during the company's Q4 FY26 earnings call in April, citing two specific U.S. clients that were "likely holding back further tech spending." In Q1 FY27, the company's Telecommunications, Technology & Services vertical — which captures work for clients like Google — declined 10.9% year-on-year, the steepest fall among all verticals.

"Since they have maintained the guidance, it roughly indicates that they do see some sort of muted growth performance in the next few quarters."

— Piyush Pandey, Senior Vice President, Centrum Broking

The Broader Industry Squeeze

Vendor consolidation is reshaping client-vendor dynamics across India's $315 billion IT services industry. Companies that win consolidation deals are gaining at the expense of those being consolidated out. Infosys and Cognizant have been among the beneficiaries, with Infosys CFO Jayesh Sanghrajka telling analysts that vendor consolidation is a "key focus" in a market where net new deals are scarce.

Cognizant's Americas President Surya Gummadi offered a nuanced take: while clients may not aim directly for consolidation, their broader goal of cost optimization leads them to reduce vendor count and focus on value-driven partnerships.

HCLTech's Q1 FY27 numbers told a mixed story. Revenue rose 13.9% year-on-year to ₹34,579 crore, and net profit jumped 20.3% to ₹4,624 crore. The company posted record first-quarter deal bookings of $2.41 billion. But in constant currency terms, revenue actually declined 0.5% sequentially — and the decision to retain its 1-4% full-year growth guidance disappointed analysts expecting an upgrade after strong bookings.

J.P. Morgan retained its "underweight" rating, citing continued weakness in discretionary technology spending. Jefferies called the unchanged guidance "the key disappointment," noting it pointed to a softer road ahead despite strong bookings. HCLTech shares fell 4.5% the day after results, wiping ₹1,480 crore ($154 million) in market capitalization.

The Diaspora Connection

For the Indian diaspora, particularly the tens of thousands of IT professionals employed by HCLTech and its peers in the U.S. and Europe, vendor consolidation translates directly to job uncertainty. HCLTech's headcount fell by 3,292 in Q1 FY27 — the sharpest quarterly drop in five quarters — to 223,889. The company added just 1,056 freshers during the period.

The dynamic is compounded by AI-driven automation. HCLTech was the first of India's big five IT firms to highlight the disconnect between revenue growth and headcount, acknowledging that AI-led productivity means fewer bodies for the same revenue. For Indian engineers on H-1B visas working at client sites in the U.S., the combination of vendor consolidation and automation represents a structural headwind that transcends any single quarter.

HCLTech's AI-First Counterstrategy

HCLTech is not standing still. Advanced AI revenue hit $172 million in Q1, up 62.1% year-on-year, with AI Force deployed across 92 client accounts. The company's board approved a ₹3,500 crore investment to build AI data centres in India, marking an entry into the full-stack AI market.

In June, HCLTech invested $150 million for a 10% stake in Sarvam AI, a Bengaluru-based sovereign AI startup — making it the first Indian IT services firm to take a significant equity position in an AI company. The company also completed its acquisition of data analytics firm JasperSoft and expanded its AI partnerships with Google Cloud and ServiceNow for Gemini Enterprise-based agent solutions.

"We expect a strong booking even in Q2. So, we feel quite positive about the overall outlook."

— C. Vijayakumar, CEO and Managing Director, HCLTech

What's Next

HCLTech's immediate challenge is demonstrating that its AI investments can offset the structural decline in top-client revenue before the trend deepens. The company has a mega deal signed in early July with a European Fortune Global 50 firm, but its revenue impact will only materialize in FY28.

For the broader Indian IT sector, the message is clear: the era of growing simply by adding more bodies to service existing accounts is ending. As clients consolidate vendors and deploy AI to automate routine IT functions, services firms must evolve from labor arbitrage plays into technology-led value creators — or risk being consolidated out of the picture themselves.
nri_angle: Vendor consolidation and AI automation directly threaten jobs for tens of thousands of Indian IT professionals on H-1B visas in the U.S. and Europe.
